newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan recovery close to self-sustaining - EPA.
newsitem.headline: Japan recovery close to self-sustaining - EPA.

text.p: Japan's economy is on the verge of a self-sustaining recovery, the Economic Planning Agency (EPA) said on Friday, in the government's strongest official assessment of the economy in the last five years.
The EPA said in its annual report that, "the present state of the economy is close to one where we can say it is recovering autonomously, led by private-sector demand."

The report said that, although the pitch of the recovery had slowed after an increase in the national sales tax to five percent from three percent in April, the recovery was not threatened and was set to continue.

While stressing it did not want to comment on whether or when interest rates should be raised, the EPA said that two years had passed since interest rates had been cut to rock-bottom levels and that firms and individuals should be aware there is a risk that interest rates may rise.
The report also said that the economy has put the worst of the hangover from the "bubble" years of inflated asset prices behind it.

While firms in industry and finance may still have balance sheet problems, these problems had slipped from a macro-economic level to a micro-economic level, losing their potential to hinder growth, the report said.
It added that healthy business cycles have been forming.
Starting from the middle of last year, inventory adjustments at firms led to a pick-up in production across broad sections of industry, which in turn helped improve employment conditions.
In addition, a weaking of the yen, which makes Japanese products cheaper to customers abroad, had led to a boom in exports.
"A relatively solid recovery is continuing," Akira Furukawa, the director of the EPA's national economic research bureau, told Reuters Financial Television in an interview.
Looking forward, the report said that the key question now was whether the recovery would lead to economic development in the medium to long term.
It said that, although the future remained unclear, the economy now had the will and stamina to embark on drastic reforms and should seize the chance to create free and transparent markets.
In particular, the report pointed to the distribution and service sectors as stifling business opportunities through over-regulation and antiquated business practices.
